opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the best way to understand the Alberta Plan is as a research roadmap rather than a recipe. It's a document that Rich Sutton, Mike Bowling, and I put together to lay out how we, here in Alberta, think about the long-term pursuit of understanding and building intelligent systems. And at its core it's really grounded in reinforcement learning, in the idea that intelligence is fundamentally about an agent interacting with a very large, complex world, taking actions, receiving observations and some kind of reward signal, and trying to learn from that ongoing stream of experience.

What makes it distinctive, I think, is the emphasis on a few key principles. The first is continual learning: the agent is never "done" training. There's no separation between a training phase and a deployment phase. The world keeps changing, the agent keeps learning, and it has to be computationally efficient enough to do that in real time. The second is that the agent is small relative to the world. It can never perfectly model everything, so it has to approximate, it has to build its own representations, its own features, its own predictive knowledge about what's going to happen next. And the third is that we want methods that scale with computation and experience rather than relying on hand-built human knowledge about a particular domain.

So the plan walks through a sequence of steps: starting with really solid foundations in continual supervised learning and prediction, moving up through learning value functions and policies, then into building models of the world, planning with those models, and ultimately getting to agents that construct abstractions in time, what we'd call options or temporally extended behaviors, and use those to reason and plan more effectively.

For me personally, a lot of my work has been in prosthetics and rehabilitation robotics, and that's where these ideas really come alive. When you have a person wearing a bionic arm, the system has to adapt to that individual, continually, every single day. It has to make predictions about what the person wants to do and work with them as a partner. That's a perfect microcosm of what the Alberta Plan is aiming at: agents that learn from experience, grow their understanding over time, and ultimately interact with people in a meaningful, collaborative way.

So I see it less as a claim that "this is how AGI will be built" and more as a statement of what we think the important questions are, and a commitment to tackling them in a principled, incremental way.

r001.rationale: The response describes the Alberta Plan as a roadmap for building intelligent agents that continually learn from their ongoing experience.

r002.rationale: It presents the plan’s principles as research commitments and describes a commitment to pursuing its questions in a principled, incremental way.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the Alberta Plan is really a research roadmap that Rich Sutton, Mike Bowling, and I put together, and the core idea is that we think about intelligence as something that emerges from a continual interaction between an agent and its world. The agent gets a stream of experience, observations and actions and rewards flowing in over time, and everything it learns, everything it knows, has to be grounded in that stream. That's the starting commitment. We're not building a system that gets a big batch of data up front and then gets frozen. We're building something that learns online, moment by moment, for its whole lifetime, and never really stops.

From there the plan lays out a sequence of steps, about a dozen of them, that go from very simple pieces up to the full agent. You start with the basics of representation and prediction from a single stream of experience, things like learning features that are useful for prediction, then move into learning value functions and policies, then into learning a model of the world so the agent can plan, and eventually into the agent discovering its own subproblems and options, its own sense of what's worth paying attention to and what's worth getting good at. Each step is meant to be a concrete, testable research problem. It's not a philosophical manifesto so much as a to-do list, and that was intentional. We wanted something that a graduate student could pick up and say, here's the piece I can work on.

The other thing I'd emphasize is what it deliberately leaves out. It's very computationally focused. We're trying to use general methods that scale with computation, in the spirit of the bitter lesson, rather than baking in a lot of human knowledge about the domain. And it's model-based in the sense that the agent should be building its own understanding of how the world works, so it can plan and imagine, rather than only reacting.

For me personally, coming from the side of working with people on prosthetic limbs and assistive devices, the appeal is that this is a vision of intelligence that is about an agent being embedded in a world with a partner, continually adapting. That's exactly what you need when a machine is working closely with a person over months and years. So I see the Alberta Plan less as a claim that we know how to get to AGI tomorrow, and more as a disciplined bet about which path is worth walking, and a set of landmarks so we know whether we're actually making progress along it.

r001.rationale: It describes the Alberta Plan as a roadmap for agents that learn continuously from their own stream of observations, actions, and rewards.

r002.rationale: It identifies guiding research commitments, including online learning grounded in experience, computationally scalable methods, and agents that build models for planning.

astra-6.text:
I think of the Alberta Plan as a research roadmap for understanding intelligence through an agent’s interaction with the world. The starting point is that an intelligent system has an ongoing stream of experience: it makes observations, takes actions, and learns from the consequences. So the question is, how do we build a system that can keep improving through that interaction?

Reinforcement learning gives us a foundation for that. But we also need to understand how an agent learns representations, builds knowledge about what might happen, and uses that knowledge to plan. Those capabilities have to work together in a system that continues learning, rather than one whose learning ends before it is deployed.

What I find compelling is the emphasis on making progress through concrete, testable steps. You start with simpler settings where you can understand the learning process, and then build toward richer capabilities and more demanding environments. The aspiration is that the same underlying principles will carry across tasks. In that sense, it’s a plan for discovering and assembling the mechanisms of general intelligence, with experience as the central resource.

r001.rationale: It describes the Alberta Plan as a roadmap for building intelligent systems that continually learn through their observations, actions, and consequences.

r002.rationale: It lays out a guiding research approach: use concrete, testable steps, progress from simpler to richer settings, and seek principles that generalize across tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I understand the Alberta Plan as a way of pursuing general intelligence by putting learning through interaction at the center. You start with an agent that acts in the world, receives observations and rewards, and has to learn from the consequences of what it does. The question is how that ongoing experience can produce increasingly capable behavior.

Reinforcement learning gives us a foundation, but there’s a lot to build around it: learning useful representations, learning how the world works, discovering useful abstractions and skills, and using those to plan. Those capabilities need to work together in an agent that continues learning, rather than having its knowledge fixed before it starts acting.

What appeals to me is that this gives us a concrete research direction. We can study the pieces, test whether they improve an agent’s ability to learn and adapt, and work toward integrating them. It’s a plan for making progress toward general intelligence, with experience as the organizing principle.

r001.rationale: It describes the Alberta Plan as pursuing general intelligence through an agent that learns from its own actions, observations, rewards, and experience.

r002.rationale: It calls the plan a concrete research direction and describes studying and integrating capabilities, but does not characterize it as a set of commitments guiding how AI research is conducted.
